title: Show HN: Hacker News, without AI
content:
The thread discusses the launch of **[hcker.news](https://hcker.news/?ai=exclude)**, a tool designed to filter AI-related content from Hacker News.

### Key Takeaways:
*   **The Problem:** Many users feel overwhelmed by the high volume of AI-related submissions, specifically branding and ads from major companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.
*   **The Solution:** The site provides an alternative view of HN by using a combination of domain/keyword filtering and a BERT-based classifier to identify and hide AI-focused content. 
*   **Community Reception:**
    *   **Positive:** Many users appreciate the ability to regain a "pre-AI" browsing experience and discover non-AI articles that would otherwise be buried.
    *   **Criticism/Nuance:** Some point out the irony of using AI to filter AI content. Others clarify that they don't necessarily hate all AI content, but rather the "slop" and repetitive marketing that dominates the front page.
    *   **Technical Feedback:** Users requested features like browser extensions, keyboard navigation improvements, and push notifications for specific topics (like "Linux"). The developer engaged with this feedback, fixing bugs and updating the code repository to include an MIT license.
*   **Alternatives:** The thread also explores other methods for managing content, including uBlock Origin custom filters, other filtering sites (like [unslop.news](https://www.unslop.news/) and [hnslop.nilsherzig.com](https://hnslop.nilsherzig.com/)), and using the native "hide" feature on Hacker News.
*   **Meta-Discussion:** There is a broader debate about the decline of post/comment quality on HN over the last decade and whether "curating" the feed through filters undermines the core concept of Hacker News.

title: Show HN: Hacker News, Without AI
content:
The thread discusses the launch of **unslop.news**, a project that filters AI-related content from the Hacker News (HN) front page. The project has sparked a mix of irony, praise, and criticism among users.

**Key points of the discussion include:**

*   **The Irony:** Users pointed out the irony that *unslop.news* is itself "vibe-coded" (built using AI) and uses an LLM to filter content, essentially using the very technology it aims to scrub. The developer confirmed this was intentional, describing it as a "layered joke."
*   **The "AI Fatigue" Debate:** Many users expressed relief at the existence of a filter, noting that the high volume of repetitive LLM-related news has diminished the diversity of content on HN. Conversely, some critics labeled these aggregator sites as "spam," noting that the recent influx of multiple "anti-AI HN" tools appearing on the front page simultaneously is ironic and counterproductive.
*   **Defining "Slop":** There is a debate regarding the scope of the filter. While some users want to avoid all AI-related news, others point out that "AI news" still constitutes a significant portion of modern tech developments. Some users argued that articles expressing "sadness" about AI are not "slop," yet are being filtered out indiscriminately.
*   **Technical Implementation:** The developer shared the project's source code, leading to lighthearted mockery regarding the project’s reliance on using regex to parse HTML—a practice often considered a "cardinal sin" in programming.
*   **Community Solutions:** The thread includes links to similar tools and suggestions for better filtering mechanisms, such as a tagging system or personal feed customization, rather than relying on external "anti-AI" mirrors.

title: Show HN: Godot and Rust based multiplexer (terminal panes and more)
content:
This thread discusses **gPTY**, a terminal multiplexer built by the OP using the **Godot game engine** and **Rust**. The project aims to provide a tileable terminal workspace with the potential for rich, non-terminal content (like media or local knowledge management) enabled by Godot’s graphical capabilities.

### Key Discussion Points:

*   **The "Why" of the Tech Stack:** Critics questioned using a heavy game engine for a terminal multiplexer, suggesting web-based technologies (Electron/Chromium) are more standard for UI. The OP and supporters argued that using Godot is an "inspired" choice that offers cross-platform support, hardware-accelerated rendering, and a departure from the "another Electron app" ecosystem.
*   **Performance & Utility:** Skeptics voiced concerns about RAM usage, terminal latency, and the general necessity of the project, with some labeling it "vibe-coded" or a solution in search of a problem. Conversely, others found the creative mashup of a game engine and terminal tools to be a great way to learn new stacks and potentially solve issues like managing autonomous AI agents.
*   **Project Maturity:**
    *   **Documentation:** The author acknowledged that the documentation currently leans heavily on LLM-generated text, which some users found verbose and hard to read, and pledged to perform a human-authored sweep.
    *   **Visuals:** Users pointed out the lack of screenshots in the README; the author agreed to improve the presentation to better showcase the tool's utility.
    *   **Accessibility:** The thread touched on the importance of accessibility; it was noted that Godot 4.5 includes integrated support for AccessKit, improving the engine's potential for professional applications.
*   **Community Sentiment:** The project sparked a polarized response. While some felt it was "useless" or artificially boosted to the front page, others defended it as a perfect example of modern, creative engineering where "atom-smashing" different technologies is encouraged, even if the result isn't a "hard" technical problem.

Overall, while gPTY is currently a hobby project, it generated significant debate over the boundaries of game engines versus general application frameworks and the role of "fun" and "experimentation" in software development.

title: Show HN: Toast, a by default in-terminal IDE
content:
The thread discusses the release of **Toast**, a "batteries-included" terminal-based IDE. The project sparked significant debate, centering on several key themes:

**1. Criticism of AI-Generated Content and Quality**
Critics pointed out that the project’s code contained obvious placeholders (e.g., `yourusername` in module paths) and inaccuracies in the README, suggesting the author relied heavily on AI without verifying the output. This led to a broader discussion on the rise of "slop"—low-quality or hastily produced projects generated by LLMs—and the frustration some developers feel toward the influx of such tools.

**2. Claims Regarding Existing Tools (Vim/Emacs)**
The README claimed that Emacs and Vim lack features like mouse support and file trees. Experienced users pushed back, noting that these features have been native or easily configurable for decades. Many commenters characterized these claims as a "skill issue" or "ignorance," emphasizing that Vim and Emacs are highly capable but require an investment in learning. The author acknowledged that their "barrier to usage" comments were poorly phrased, clarifying that they aimed to provide an intuitive, out-of-the-box experience for those who do not want to spend hours customizing their environment.

**3. Terminal IDE Philosophy**
The discussion touched on the trend of moving development environments into the terminal. Supporters appreciate the reduced resource usage and the ability to keep everything in one interface. Detractors argue that terminal-based UIs are often inferior to GUI-based IDEs (like VS Code or those built with Qt), claiming they lack the polish, interactive features (inline images, rich links), and integration capabilities of modern GUI applications.

**4. Author's Context**
The developer of Toast candidly shared that they built the project using AI due to the time constraints of raising young children, admitting that the project was a way to ship something personal despite limited bandwidth. While this generated empathy from some, others maintained that personal limitations do not justify the distribution of poorly vetted, "slop-filled" code to the public.

title: Show HN: ResolveHQ – A Helpdesk Built on Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2 and Queues
content:
The thread features the launch of **ResolveHQ**, an open-source helpdesk platform built on the Cloudflare stack (Workers, D1, R2, and Queues).

**Key discussion points:**

*   **Feedback on Presentation:** The community strongly encouraged the developer to add screenshots or a demo to the README, noting that the project's usability is currently difficult to gauge without visual context.
*   **Alternative Solutions:** Several users shared their own similar projects (e.g., *StayUpFront*, *Sluice*, *Projektor*, *GoodSupport*) or established alternatives like *Freescout*. There is clear interest in lightweight, self-hosted, or simplified helpdesk and ticketing solutions that avoid the complexity of tools like Jira.
*   **Technical Challenges:** Experienced developers in the thread highlighted common hurdles when building custom support tools, specifically:
    *   **Email Threading:** The difficulty of maintaining conversation continuity due to providers modifying `Message-ID` or `In-Reply-To` headers.
    *   **Webhook Reliability:** Managing duplicates and redeliveries from incoming event triggers.
    *   **Automation:** Discussions around integrating AI (LLMs) for automated responses, translation, and ticket management.
*   **Infrastructure Trends:** Users noted the efficiency of building on Cloudflare’s native email and serverless infrastructure, with some debating the necessity of third-party email wrappers like Resend now that Cloudflare offers native email services.
